name: Yohimbine fasted training

lead: Lean-physique athletes use yohimbine, an alpha-2 adrenergic blocker from yohimbe bark, around training done without recent food. The aim is a leaner midsection and visibly lower body fat, with fasting intended to keep insulin low while the compound is active.

Yohimbine acts as an antagonist at alpha-2 receptors and increases noradrenaline release.[1] Wikipedia notes that there is very little published research supporting bodybuilding and weight-loss claims for yohimbe supplements.[1]

paras: Bodybuilders on contest-prep logs describe it as one tool among several, alongside very low calories, caffeine, fasting and walking.[2] Some users also discuss topical forms intended for stubborn areas.[3] No dosing is given here.

Yohimbine can cause high blood pressure, fast heart rate, anxiety, tremor and nausea, and has been linked to cardiovascular problems and seizures.[1] Supplements are often mislabeled and regulators have warned about yohimbe products.[1]

lead: Yohimbine fasted training is a practice in physique-building circles of combining yohimbine, a plant alkaloid sold as a supplement, with exercise performed while fasted. The appearance goal is shedding stubborn fat to look leaner and more defined.

Yohimbine comes from the bark of the African tree Pausinystalia johimbe and blocks alpha-2 adrenergic receptors, which increases release of noradrenaline.[1] Users on T Nation describe it within cutting stacks, one listing it among caffeine, an ECA stack, fasting and very low calories.[2] Another discussion mentions topical yohimbine used to target specific fat areas.[3]

Wikipedia reports that virtually no published research supports bodybuilding or weight-loss claims for yohimbe supplements, and that regulators including the FDA, Health Canada and EFSA have acted on or commented about them.[1]

paras: The practice joins a stimulant-like supplement to fasted exercise. It appears in cutting logs where users list yohimbine among fat-loss aids.[2]

Yohimbine has high affinity for alpha-2 receptors, which it antagonises, and also binds alpha-1, serotonin and dopamine D2 receptors. Oral bioavailability averages about 33%, and half-life is roughly 15 minutes to 2.5 hours.[1]

Adolph Spiegel first extracted yohimbine in 1896 and the first total synthesis was completed in 1958.[1] Yohimbe bark was used in folk medicine as an aphrodisiac, and since the 1970s yohimbine has been used in veterinary medicine to reverse xylazine.[1]

Yohimbine has been studied for erectile dysfunction and PTSD, with insufficient evidence in the Wikipedia summary.[1] The same article says there is virtually no published research for bodybuilding claims.[1] In 2007 a WADA case involved an athlete who tested positive for a steroid metabolite after reportedly taking yohimbine.[1]

High doses can cause hypertension, tachycardia, agitation, tremors and nausea, and interactions can cause serious cardiovascular events.[1] A 2022 Tennessee Poison Center warning described potentially fatal effects, and content in US supplements is highly variable.[1] Canada removed yohimbe products in 2019 and the UK bans yohimbe herbal supplements.[1]
No studies found on the combination with fasted training specifically.
